idiom_name: scope placement with private/fileprivate/internal/package plus a same-file attorney type; @testable import where the grant exists only for tests
implementation_notes: Swift's access levels are declaration-, file-, module- and package-scoped: private restricts an entity to its enclosing declaration and to extensions of that declaration in the same file, fileprivate to the file, internal to the module, and package to the package (The Swift Programming Language, Access Control). There is no friend-to-type declaration, so what replaces the classic structure is placement: keep the implementation private (or fileprivate when a separate attorney type in the same file must reach it), expose only the granted method, and use internal when the helper lives elsewhere in the module. Because an entity cannot be defined in terms of a less accessible type, the granted surface must be expressible in types at least as visible as itself, which bounds how narrow the attorney can be.
pitfalls: private covers the enclosing declaration and its same-file extensions, not 'the type': a second type in the file needs fileprivate, so letting an attorney exist usually widens the grant to the whole file.

Access levels constrain signatures, so a private implementation type cannot appear in a public attorney's API - keep it out, or the boundary leaks through the signature (and the compiler will refuse the declaration).
@testable import hands the test module every internal entity, which is why tests rarely need the attorney - and tests that reach in anyway become coupled to implementation details.
